column2: Tilt a book a quarter turn about one line on the table. Then roll it a quarter turn about another. Now swap the order. Roll first, then tilt. Does the book end up the same way?
No. Tilt first, and the cover ends up facing you. Roll first, and it faces the wall on your right.
Sliding is nothing like this. Slide the book right, then away, or away, then right. Same spot. Positions add. Orientations don't.
This is a KUKA robot arm with seven joints. Its job is to put its gripper at a pose, a position and an orientation together.
So its software must do arithmetic with things that refuse to add. The way out is about a hundred and fifty years old, and by the end you'll read it in one line.
Look where tilt then roll left the book. It could have got there in a single turn, about a single axis.
Two quarter turns went in. How big is that single turn?
A third of a turn. Three of them bring the book home. Its axis leans equally from the book's three edges.
That always works. Any turn followed by any turn is one turn about one axis. Euler showed it in seventeen seventy-five.
And any turn can be undone. A collection where you can combine any two, and undo any one, is called a group. In this one, order usually matters.
To compute, track where the book's three edges point. Three arrows, three numbers each. Nine numbers in a grid, a matrix. One turn after another is one grid times another.
Nine numbers is a lot for one orientation. Three should do. Here is a machine that tries, a gimbal. Three rings, one inside the next, each turning about its own axis.
Turn the middle ring a quarter turn. Now the outer ring's axis and the inner ring's axis line up. Do those two rings still do different things?
No. They turn the book about the very same axis. Nothing is stuck, but three rings now give only two ways to turn. This is gimbal lock.
Apollo flew with it. Its guidance platform hung in three gimbals. Past seventy degrees on the middle one, a warning lamp lit. Past eighty-five, the computer dropped its sense of direction.
On Apollo eleven, Michael Collins radioed a request. How about sending me a fourth gimbal for Christmas. With a fourth ring, there is always one to spare.
It wasn't bad engineering. Name every orientation with just three numbers, and somewhere there is a bad spot. So software stores nine numbers, or four. The spare ones are the price.
Angles hide a second trap. Take two headings for a robot. A hundred and seventy degrees to the left. And a hundred and seventy to the right, written minus a hundred and seventy.
What heading is halfway between them?
Average the numbers and you get zero. Straight ahead. But both arrows point almost straight back. The honest halfway is a hundred and eighty, the exact opposite.

The trouble is the ruler's seam. So peel the ruler off, and lay it flat against the circle, with its zero on the first heading. Now measure to the second. Twenty degrees. Take half. Ten degrees on from the first is a hundred and eighty.
That is the whole trick, and the rest of this video is that trick again and again. The space is curved. Do the arithmetic on the flat piece that touches it. Then wrap the answer back on.

On the circle, a step along the flat piece was so many degrees. Read it as a speed, held for one second. In space, the flat piece is made of such spins, each one arrow, along its axis, as long as its speed.
Arrows are easy to stretch, to average and to add. But adding two spins is not one turn then another. It is both at once.
Hold one spin steady for one second, and the book ends at some orientation. That step, from the flat piece back to the curved space, is the exponential.
Spin the book about the line leaning equally from its three edges, a third of a turn per second. After one second, where do its edges point?
Each edge lands where the next one was. That is where the book ended in the first quiz, with roll first.
The step has a formula, named after Rodrigues. Any point splits into a part along the axis, which stays, and a part that swings around.
A group of motions that is smooth like this is a Lie group, after the Norwegian mathematician Sophus Lie. Its flat piece is its Lie algebra.

Poses work the same way. Start on a floor, with a KUKA mobile platform. Its wheels carry slanted rollers, so it can drive forward, slide sideways and spin, all at once. Three numbers for its pose, three for its velocity.
Hold one velocity for six seconds. Forward at half a meter per second, spinning at thirty degrees per second. Where does the platform end up?
Beside where it started. Just under two meters to its left, facing backward. It drove a half circle.

Add six seconds of velocity onto the pose, and you predict three meters straight ahead. That is the flat piece's answer. Wrap it onto the curved space, and the same three meters bend around a fixed point.
Now leave the floor. On a floor, a pose could change in three independent ways. Forward, sideways, and turning. In how many ways can a pose change in space?
Six. Three slides and three turns. So a velocity in space is two arrows, a slide and a spin. Six numbers, which roboticists call a twist.
Hold a twist steady, and you get the motion of a screw. The body turns about an axis, and slides along that same axis.
A door is a screw with no slide. A drawer is a screw with no turn. A bottle cap does both.
Here is the surprise. Pick up the book. Put it down anywhere, facing any way. One screw would have carried it there. Every time.
Michel Chasles published that in eighteen thirty. Giulio Mozzi had described such an axis in seventeen sixty-three.
Back to the arm. Standing straight up, it is one point three meters tall. Each of its seven joints is a hinge, like the door. All it can do is turn about its own axis.
A turn about an axis is a screw with no slide. So the arm is seven screws, stacked.
Suppose only joint four turns, the elbow. Which parts of the arm move?
Everything past the elbow, as one rigid piece. Nothing before it. Each joint applies its screw to everything further out.

That gives a recipe for the arithmetic. Start with the gripper's pose when every joint is at zero. Apply the last joint's screw, then the one before, down to the first. That way, each axis is still at its zero place when its turn comes.
Each screw, held for its joint angle, is an exponential. So the gripper's pose is a product of seven exponentials, the line from the start. Roger Brockett presented it in nineteen eighty-three.
Try it by hand, with the real arm's lengths.
Bend two joints a quarter turn each, the shoulder and the elbow. The recipe says, elbow first. With the arm still straight up, the elbow's screw swings the forearm over until it lies level.
Then the shoulder's screw swings everything, about the shoulder's axis, just where it stood at zero. The upper arm comes down level, and the forearm points straight up.
Now joint one, at the base, turns a quarter turn about the vertical. Where does the gripper go?
Round to the side, at the same height. It was forty-two centimeters in front of the base. Now it is forty-two centimeters to the side.
Notice what the recipe never asked. Where the elbow's axis is now. Each screw is written down once, with the arm at zero.
Here is the question a robot really faces. This is the pose I want. Which joint angles get me there? The answer starts with speeds.
For speeds, each axis counts where it is right now. A joint turning alone swings the gripper around its axis. That is a twist. And twists live on the flat piece, so they add.
Seven joints, seven twists, six numbers each. Stand them side by side. A grid, six rows by seven columns, called the Jacobian. Joint speeds go in. The gripper's twist comes out.
The arm is in an L shape. Which joint moves the gripper's tip fastest, at the same turning speed? Joint one, two or seven?

Joint two. What counts is how far the tip is from each axis. Sixty-seven centimeters from the shoulder's. Forty-two from the base's. And the tip sits right on joint seven's axis, so that joint only spins it.
Six rows allow six independent directions for the gripper. Usually, seven joints cover all six.
Here the arm's elbow is straight. Can the gripper still move in all six directions?
No. Along the arm, every joint's push on the wrist is zero. So the gripper can't slide further out, and it can't even begin to slide straight back. Five of the six directions are left.
A pose like this is called a singularity. Close to one, a motion along the lost direction costs huge joint speeds.

Pull the gripper straight back at ten centimeters per second. With the elbow bent thirty degrees, it must turn at fifty-four degrees per second. Bent ten degrees, a hundred and sixty. Its limit is seventy-five.

You have met this before. The wrist is three joints whose axes meet at one point, a gimbal. Straighten it, and two axes line up, like the rings. A six-joint arm would lose a direction here. The seventh joint covers for it.
Seven joints. Six directions. One joint is spare. What does it buy?
Try it on yourself. Lay your palm flat on a desk and keep your shoulder still. Can your elbow still move?
It can. It swings on an arc while your hand stays put. Counted the way a roboticist counts, your arm has seven joints too.
The robot does the same. Its gripper holds one pose, while its elbow swings on a circle twenty-nine centimeters in radius.
That is what the spare joint buys. The elbow can get out of the way while the gripper keeps working.
Back to the question. Here is the pose I want. Which joint angles get me there?
Subtracting angles walks into both traps. These two orientations are one point four degrees apart. Yet two of their three ring angles differ by ninety.
So do it on the flat piece. Compare the pose the arm has with the pose it wants. One screw joins them. Read as a twist, that screw is the error.
Then run the Jacobian backwards, from that twist to joint speeds, and move the joints that way. Look again, and repeat.
The gripper starts half a meter from its goal, and a quarter turn off. How many steps until it is within a tenth of a millimeter?
From this start, three. Half a meter off. Then nine centimeters. Then four millimeters. Then three hundredths of a millimeter. It is Newton's method, on a curved space.
One more question. Between the start and the goal, what should the gripper do on the way?
Blend the two orientations, number by number. Half of one matrix plus half of the other. Is the result halfway there?
It is not even an orientation. A gripper turned by that blend would be squashed to half its volume.

The honest path is the screw. Do the halving on the flat piece. Take the twist that joins the two poses, and hold it for half a second. Half the turn and half the slide, and every pose on the way is a true pose.
The tip may go straight instead, because positions do add. Here the two paths differ by seven point six centimeters.

The same moves run far beyond this arm. Drones steer poses. Mapping robots average them. A physics engine steps each body by the exponential of a small twist, so it stays rigid. And a humanoid's whole body floats as one free pose, plus twenty-nine joint angles.
Last one. Tilt the book one degree, then roll it one degree. Then the other order. Do the two results still differ?
They do, by less than two hundredths of a degree. And that leftover is itself a turn, almost exactly about the one axis neither turn used.

For small turns, make both ten times smaller, and the leftover shrinks a hundredfold. On the flat piece, that leftover follows a rule of its own, called the Lie bracket. It measures how much order matters.
So the arm does not add orientations. It multiplies motions, and does its adding on the flat piece. That is what it means to think in Lie groups.
